extracted.intended_audience: NLP / computational humour researchers and practitioners (LLM developers, computational linguists)
extracted.subtask_description: Survey of methods, evaluation, and future directions for generating and explaining humour (puns, topical jokes, memes, etc.) using NLP and LLMs. Focuses on modelling requirements, evaluation paradigms, and ethical/practical considerations for humour systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour requires violation of expectation (incongruity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary feature of humorous language is that it violates an expectation within the reader, either in the form of cultural or situational norms (e.g., topical and contextual humour), or linguistic norms (e.g., puns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This core property poses a challenge to computational approaches because the language modelling objective aims to maximise likelihood, working against the incongruity humour demands. Example: jokes exploiting phonetic similarity or cultural references rely on surprisal/incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity Theory / norm violation as computationally tractable basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity Theory states that humour is the perception of something that conflicts with established mental patterns and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The survey argues incongruity and norm violation remain essential elements for computational approaches; these are more easily operationalised than Relief or Superiority theories for linguistic models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Benign Violation Theory postulates that humour arises from situations that are simultaneously harmless (benign) and incongruous with expectations (violating a norm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for modelling risk-to-reward tradeoffs in generation: sensitive topics may increase humour for intended audience but increase risk of offence for others; guides demographic-aware generation and safety considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief and Superiority theories (conceptual frameworks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief Theory (humour as release of psychological energy) and Superiority Theory (humour from perceiving one individual as superior to another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes these theories 'do not present simple interpretations that can be easily formulated linguistically and computationally', so are less directly useful as generation/evaluation rubrics compared to incongruity-based approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homographic pun requirement: support multiple senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Homographic puns exploit polysemy: the model must generate sentences that could support the semantics of two word senses simultaneously (i.e., produce semantic ambiguity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches include constrained decoding to jointly decode two senses, discriminators for word-sense support, training on sense-aware objectives. Evaluation measures include human judgements of whether both senses are supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterographic pun requirement: phonetic similarity + semantic coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterographic puns require modelling phonetic similarity between different surface forms while maintaining semantic coherence in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems must infer phonetic relationships from text or use phonetic resources; approaches include retrieve-and-edit frameworks and insertion of foreshadowing topic words to create global association (local-global surprisal). Models struggle more with heterographic puns due to lacking phonetic knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined pun attributes: ambiguity, distinctiveness, surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: A unified framework should incorporate three linguistic attributes: ambiguity, distinctiveness, and surprise to address both homographic and heterographic pun generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and evaluation should measure these attributes; e.g., ambiguity = ability to support multiple senses, distinctiveness = separation of competing meanings, surprise = unexpectedness/low probability given context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'lazy pun generation' (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lazy pun generation: models incorporate both senses of the pun word in a single generation (nullifying surprisal), e.g., 'The sailor’s pay was docked after he struggled to dock on time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generation systems should avoid explicit inclusion of both meanings in one utterance; evaluation should detect and penalise this behaviour since it removes required cognitive effort for humour resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-situated pun generation (CUP): contextual awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate puns naturally into real-world conversations by demanding contextual awareness (extracting keywords from context and generating sentences that support both meanings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CUP-style tasks use keyword extraction (e.g., RAKE) and conditional generation (T5) to ensure puns fit conversational context; evaluation should test coherence with preceding turns and plausibility in dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Template preservation for set-up/punchline jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: For set-up and punchline style jokes, maintain essential structure via template extraction and infilling so generated instances preserve joke shape while allowing topic flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mask tokens based on attention weights to determine which elements to keep; use infilling with LLMs to create novel jokes. Evaluation should assess whether the structure is preserved and punchline delivers surprisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetic/phonemic information inclusion for phonetic humour and tongue twisters
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks relying on pronunciation (tongue twisters, phonetic puns) benefit from incorporation of explicit phonetic and phonemic information into generation models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches train on graphemes or phonemes and/or augment with phonetic resources; evaluation should measure pronounceability, intended difficulty, and humour/entertainment from phonetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical and cultural knowledge retrieval for topical humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical jokes depend on esoteric, timely world knowledge and cultural references, requiring advanced retrieval and contextual grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should link to real-world sources (Wikipedia, news) and handle post-training events; evaluation must check factual/contextual accuracy and whether the punchline relies on retrievable topical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection/classification as precursor to explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour detection (assigning labels like pun type, irony, sarcasm) is a useful precursor to explanation because it identifies linguistic traits common to humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification approaches include WSD for puns and BERT/ensemble classifiers for genre/technique; limitations: classification is coarse, requires taxonomy creation, and offers limited help to end-users seeking human-friendly explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy quality and overlap concerns in classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a robust high-quality taxonomy of humour types is challenging: categories overlap (e.g., irony vs sarcasm vs incongruity vs 'wit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary when using classification as explanation; evaluation and dataset design should acknowledge category overlap and subjectivity; prefer flexible or hierarchical taxonomies and consider perspectivist approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural language explanation as stronger evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural language explanations provide tailored, specific accounts of why a text is humorous and test deeper model understanding beyond taxonomy labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generating NL explanations is more challenging and expensive to evaluate (needs human judgements) but reduces chance of accidental success that plagues detection; use chain-of-thought prompting, in-context learning, and human preference judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal information improves humour understanding and explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to visual or audio modalities (images, speech audio) improves models' ability to explain multimodal humour (memes, cartoons) and phonetic jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: visual cues improved cartoon explanation in 84.7% of cases (human preference); adding speech audio yielded ~2.5–4% improvement for phonetic joke explanations. Design multimodal pipelines and evaluate with human preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-authored explanations remain preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when finetuning or in-context learning is used, human-authored explanations are still preferred by humans in a majority of cases (e.g., preferred in 68% of instances over best model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human explanation corpora for training/finetuning and rely on human evaluation (preference judgements) rather than only automatic metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic-aware / audience-tailored generation to reduce offence
rubrics_metrics.description: Future systems should be audience-tailored and demographic-aware to better address preferences and decrease the risk of generating offensive material for a given end-user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate human preference alignment techniques such as RLHF, DPO, and PPO; leverage perspectivist datasets and model individual preferences to manage risk-to-reward tradeoffs in humour topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-in-the-loop generation to preserve creative authorship and reduce harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote systems that require meaningful user contributions or assist in joke workshopping rather than generating jokes wholesale, to mitigate ethical risks and impacts on creative industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interfaces and algorithms that support co-creation, feedback loops, and constrained generation; evaluate by measuring user satisfaction, perceived helpfulness, and preservation of human authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent-aware explanation and intent description generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the characteristics and intent of the author (based on prior language use or inferred demographics) before explaining humour, to better infer ambiguous references and flag when 'it's just a joke' masks hateful intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop intent-annotated datasets and benchmarks (e.g., MemeIntent); evaluation should measure correct intent inference and ethical flagging (e.g., cyberbullying detection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design evaluation to target complex, context-sensitive humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus explanation and evaluation research on context-sensitive, esoteric, topical jokes, which present rich challenges for retrieval and commonsense reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct datasets drawn from social media/Reddit topical jokes; evaluate retrieval accuracy, reference disambiguation, and final explanation quality under human judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal meme explanation goals can include entertaining explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: When generating explanations for memes, one valid objective is producing explanations that entertain and amuse readers rather than being strictly objective accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide evaluation objectives (objective correctness vs entertaining value) and collect human judgements that measure both informativeness and entertainment; be aware of ethical tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic detection metrics are vulnerable; explanation reduces accidental success
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection approaches are objective and automatable but susceptible to statistical flukes; natural language explanation has a vanishingly low probability of accidentally producing coherent comedic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanation-based evaluations for deep understanding claims; when using automatic metrics, complement with human evaluations and robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-identification of pun word limits practicality of WSD-based explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning sense keys to a pun word requires the pun word to be pre-identified, which nullifies practical appropriateness of such systems in unconstrained settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should include pun localization/identification components or use end-to-end explanation approaches that do not assume pre-specified pun locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance observation: heterographic puns are harder than homographic puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Large language models struggle considerably more with heterographic puns than homographic puns, likely due to the need to infer phonetic characteristics from text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluation axis; consider augmenting models with phonetic resources or multimodal audio to improve heterographic pun handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of human preference alignment techniques for better generation quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply RLHF, Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO), PPO and other human-alignment methods to align generation systems with human preferences for humour content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate preference datasets, reward modelling, and curriculum learning; evaluate via human preference judgements and downstream safety/alignments (offensiveness reduction).
